I think that anything that gives one pleasure can become an addiction, but that some things are more addicting than others. I have no sources to cite here, there is purely a personal opinion based on my limited range of experiences in life.

I'm afraid this is a bit of a nonstarter. The existence of video game addiction cannot really be argued in favor or against any more than the existence of gravity or internet controversy. Anything that triggers mood elevation can be addictive. That doesn't mean that because something can be addicting that it will be addicting.

I don't have a strong compulsion to drink alcohol, so I can do it regularly without incident. Alcoholism runs in my family, though, so I have to be mindful of my potential for abuse. I know TV addicts, movie addicts, food addicts, drug addicts, sugar addicts, soda addicts, exercise addicts, game addicts, internet addicts, book addicts, collection addicts, achievement point addicts, attention addicts, and drama addicts. None of them are overly flawed in such ways that I would need to end my friendship and/or association with them.

You could argue that video game addiction is a chiefly harmless addiction, or even a mildly beneficial one. The kind of consumption/participation experienced is usually to some extent a brain-strengthening exercise, but that isn't always the case (there are the occasional mindless games). However, nowadays, in a world that has embraced the concept of freemium and in-game cash shops with open arms, gaming addiction can be highly destructive force. I've spent just north of $500 on Guild Wars 2's gem shop over the last few years since its launch, but there are people that spend over $500 a month on it.

If someone has never struggled with addiction, it might be hard to recognize. It's something uniquely alienating; a feeling of self-directed betrayal that you simply cannot seem to consistently overpower this unrelenting compulsion. It takes almost a complete internal reconstruction to overpower it. Most cannot do it alone, and need counsel and a supportive network.

However, if someone makes efforts to be a well-rounded person with multiple interests and hobbies, I think video games are more of a beneficial diversion than a harmful one. If someone only has the consumption of (or participation with) electronic media (or art) in its various forms as the entire breadth of their hobbies, I strongly encourage them to look through the vast catalog of interests and hobbies and find one or two that suits them. It may not necessarily be an addiction, but it never hurts to be more well-rounded.
